description:
Data Standardizer provides implementations of various internationally recognised standards in data processing, covering topics ranging from languages to currencies and geographical entities. With strongly-typed enumerations for each standard (where applicable) or other targeted data types, you can represent these elements in your code such that errors with invalid values are minimised.

Provides types supporting the reading and writing of files in standard formats.  Includes:
- Comma Separated Value (CSV).  Supports reading and writing CSV files with customizable delimiters. Ideal for CSV data normalization and transformation workflows.
releaseNotes:
Breaking changes:
- A `CsvFileRecordLine` property that calls `GetPropertyValue<T>` throws `InvalidCastException` when its field holds another type's value instead of returning the default; map the property to convert it.
- A header handler must return as many field names as each record is expected to have, none of them null, or `ReadLine` throws `InvalidOperationException`.
- With `CsvFileHeaderHandling.Ignore` and a header handler, a header line that repeats a field name makes `ReadLine` throw `CsvFileException`.
- `CsvFileWriter` throws `ArgumentException` for options whose output can't be read back: an empty or `null` `TerminatorLineBreak`, a `FieldDelimiterCharacter` that is a quote or starts the terminator, a terminator starting with a quote, or an undefined `QuoteHandling`.
- On .NET Standard, `CsvFileWriter.WriteLine` throws `InvalidOperationException`, and writes nothing, when the options have been changed to such values.
- `CsvFileReader` reports a field holding a control character, such as TAB, or a character outside its encoding as a bad value, and `CsvFileWriter` throws `CsvFileException` for one, as RFC 4180 `TEXTDATA` requires.
- `CsvFileWriter.WriteLine` throws `InvalidOperationException` when the field delimiter or terminator holds a character its encoding can't write, or `EmbeddedLineBreak` one that isn't printable in it.
- Without a header line, a field mapped by name takes the first position no other mapping takes, so one mapped after a field index fills the gap below that index.
- `CsvFileWriter` throws `CsvFileException` for a header line with no field for a required mapping by name, which a reader with the same mapper couldn't read.
- A mapping of a field the file doesn't have no longer reads the value another mapping's constant or generator adds for it: an optional one is skipped, a required one throws `CsvFileException`.
- `CsvFileReader` reports a field holding a lone surrogate, or bytes that aren't valid in the file's encoding, as a bad value, instead of reading U+FFFD or `?`.
- `CsvFileReader` reads a file in `CsvFileOptions.Encoding` even when it starts with the byte order mark of another encoding.

New:
- `UseFieldName` on a field mapping, and `CsvFieldMappingAttribute.UseFieldName`, give a field the name it is known by once read; `CsvFileWriter` writes it under its name in the file.

Fixed:
- A property mapped to a field with another name now reads and writes that field's value.
- A property mapped by index reads the field at that position of the record, not another column.
- A required mapping whose field the record doesn't have, by name or by index, throws `CsvFileException` instead of giving the property its default value.
- `CsvFileWriter.WriteLine` writes nothing for a line that `InconsistentFieldCountHandler` handled, instead of a blank record.
- Without a header line, a record line that `CsvFileWriter.WriteLine` handled as inconsistent or threw for no longer adds its fields to later lines.
- Without a header line, `CsvFileWriter.WriteLine` no longer drops the value of a field the first record line doesn't have; it handles the line as an inconsistent field count.
- `CsvFileWriter` with `SuppressTrailingBlankFields` no longer drops values or keeps blanks when a record line's fields are in another order.
- `CsvFileReader` rejects a quoted field the file ends inside, whitespace around a quoted field, and a CR or LF in an unquoted field (RFC 4180 section 2), calling `BadValueHandler` or throwing `CsvFileException`.
- `CsvFieldConvertFromString` and `CsvFieldValidate` contexts give the field's raw value and position, and `CsvFieldConvertToString` contexts the position and name of the field written.
- `ConvertUsing` delegates and type converters configured for a `string` property now run on read and write, instead of being skipped.
- Mapping covers inherited properties and their attributes, so a `[CsvField]` or `[CsvFieldMapping]` on a base class applies to derived record lines and models.
- `CsvFileReader` no longer throws `ArgumentException` when a header or mapped field is named like a generated `Field N`; it reports an inconsistent field count or renames the generated field `Field N (2)`.
- `CsvFileWriter` no longer drops a record line's fields that aren't in the header line or mapper; a field not in the header line makes the line inconsistent.
- CsvFileWriter writes a constant or generated mapping's value when the line doesn't hold the field.
- `CsvFileReader` and `CsvFileWriter` throw `ArgumentException` for a `BadValueHandler`, `InconsistentFieldCountHandler` or `HeaderHandler` of a type they never call, instead of ignoring it.
- `ToObject` and `ToCsvLine` apply the whole custom mapper, not just its field names.
- A mapped `ConstantValue` of another number type, such as `5` on a `long` property, converts to the property's type, and one the type can't hold, such as `-1` on a `byte`, throws `CsvFileException`, instead of reading as the default.
- A TypeConverter that can't convert from a string no longer makes the reader give the default value; the built-in parse reads the field instead.
- `CsvFileWriter` writes a `DateTime`, `DateTimeOffset`, `DateOnly` or `TimeOnly` it has no converter for with the round-trip pattern (`"o"`), keeping fractional seconds, `Kind` and offset.
- `CsvFileWriter` writes a `double` or `float` it has no converter for in the fewest digits that read back as the same value, as the same text on every target.
- A header handler is called whatever the header handling, with the file's header line; with `CsvFileHeaderHandling.Use` it was ignored, and with `Ignore` passed null.
- A `Map().Property()` mapping of a property with `[CsvField]` uses the field that attribute names for reading, writing and its key, as a declarative mapping does.
- `CsvFileWriter.WriteLine` no longer writes a header or record line with no fields as an empty line; it throws `CsvFileException`, or calls `InconsistentFieldCountHandler` for a record line.
- On .NET Standard, `CsvFileOptions` and `CsvFieldContext<TModel>` compare by value and print their properties from `ToString`, as on .NET 10.
- `CsvFileWriter` writes a field mapped by index at its index, so the same mapper reads the file back.
- Properties of different types mapped to the same field each read the field's value, instead of 0 and null.
- `CsvFileReader` reads a header line that repeats a field name, as RFC 4180 allows, when the mapper gives each field of that name a name of its own.
- CsvFileReader reads a double or float as its nearest value on .NET Framework.
- `CsvFileWriter` writes a mapped property's own value when its field name or `[CsvField]` name is another property's `[CsvField]` key, instead of that property's value.
- `CsvFileWriter` throws `CsvFileException`, not `EncoderFallbackException`, for a value that holds a lone surrogate.
- A property of a line read through a mapping reads as not set when the record has no field for it, instead of the value of another field named like its `[CsvField]` key.

Changed:
- `SuppressTrailingBlankFields` judges a trailing field by the text written for it: a converter writing nothing leaves it out, and a constant or generated value is written.
- `ToObject` no longer falls back to the field named after the property when the mapping names a field the line doesn't have.
- A `DateTime` field with a UTC designator (`Z` or `GMT`) reads as UTC, with `DateTimeKind.Utc`, instead of being converted to the machine's local time.
- On `net10.0`, a `DateOnly` field in the round-trip pattern (`yyyy-MM-dd`) reads as that Gregorian date in every culture.
- `CsvFileWriter` puts a header line's index-mapped fields at their indexes, its other mapped fields in the gaps and unmapped ones last, and a record line's unmapped fields in the gaps.
